147	
148	# Writing pack prose
149	
150	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
151	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
152	
153	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
154	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
155	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
156	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
157	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
158	
159	## The ration
160	
161	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
162	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
163	
164	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
165	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
166	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
167	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
168	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
169	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
170	  trigger.
171	- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
172	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
173	  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
174	  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs on the element's
175	  provenance file (below).
176	- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
177	  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
178	  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
179	  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads.
180	- **Starting a `SKILL.md`, or editing one that declares no body** — say under its frontmatter
181	  `metadata` what the body is: `body: workflow` for a procedure, whose steps and their gotchas
182	  change as one, or `body: guidelines` for rules behind a trigger, kept on the skill's one file
183	  until one has a history of its own. A skill that mixes the two declares the shape of its
184	  greater part. The harness ignores the key; the corpus's own maintenance reads it, and never
185	  infers it.
186	
187	## Shape a rule so it fires
188	
189	- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
190	  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
191	  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
192	  reader to it.
193	- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
194	  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
195	  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
196	- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
197	  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
198	  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
199	- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
200	  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
201	- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
202	  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
203	  to three neighbouring bullets.
204	- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
205	  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
206	  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
207	- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
208	  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
209	- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
210	  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
211	  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
212	- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
213	  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
214	  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
215	  you report the change.
216	- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
217	  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
218	- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
219	  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
220	  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
221	  it.
222	- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
223	  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
224	  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
225	- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
226	  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
227	  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
228	  hand-built command.
229	- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
230	  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
231	- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
232	  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
233	- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
234	  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
235	  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
236	  reader doesn't need at act time goes on the element's provenance file (below).
237	- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
238	  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
239	  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
240	  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
241	  teaches a world the reader won't find.
242	- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
243	  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.
244	
245	## The provenance log - where a rule's rationale lives
246	
247	A pack keeps one file per element under `provenance/`, beside its `RULES.md`: an append-only
248	log of the decisions behind the element, read by maintenance and review - the pass that asks
249	whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written - and never by a session.
250	No rule sends its reader there, nothing loads it, and it never vendors: a member mounting a
251	canon pack receives the rules, not the reasoning behind them. The grammar, the kinds, the
252	fields and the tool are [changing-pack-elements](../changing-pack-elements/SKILL.md)'s; what
253	this skill adds is how a rule is written so the log can hold it.
254	
255	- **Ending a rule** - every rule in a `RULES.md` ends with the bare marker naming its file -
256	  `… never a filesystem walk. (url-filter-host-operators)` - and nothing else: don't name the
257	  folder, don't link it, don't ask the reader to follow anything. The marker is the element's
258	  id: two to four hyphenated words for the guideline rather than its wording, chosen once and
259	  never renamed, so a rewording never touches it and a member's override can name it. Two
260	  rules whose history is one may share a marker. A guidelines skill's bullets are the skill's
261	  file's and carry none, until one's history diverges and it takes a marker and a file of its
262	  own; a workflow skill's steps carry none, the skill being the element.
263	- **Adding a rule** - write the brief rule and end it with its marker; create its file with a
264	  `born` entry through `provenance.mjs append` (`mark` creates the file where none exists),
265	  and put the reason there, never in the rule. A consequence the reader needs under pressure
266	  earns its clause; rationale the reader doesn't need at act time is the entry's. Write the
267	  entry so a future review can **reaffirm the rule from it** - `Retire when` is what would
268	  have to be true for the rule to go.
269	  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
270	    the error, the measured cost).
271	  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
272	  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it - in a member's
273	    local pack; a canon file carries the paraphrase, never the quote.
274	- **Rewording, moving, splitting or converting a rule** - the entry is owed in the same
275	  change, and the forced skill names its kind.
276	- **A check's rationale** - on the check's own file, named by its id (`cer/version-bumped` →
277	  `cer-version-bumped.md`); nothing is added to the check.
278	- **Removing a rule or check** - its file stays and gains a `retired` entry as its last, in
279	  the same change.
280	
281	The `provenance-integrity` check holds the mechanism together - every carrier names a live
282	file, every file parses - and `provenance-change-recorded` holds the change: a carrier that
283	changed lands with its entry. A pack not yet on the convention is put there by
284	`provenance.mjs mark`, and its history filled by the
285	[backfilling-provenance](../backfilling-provenance/SKILL.md) skill; nothing here is done rule by
286	rule.
287	
288	## Evidence
289	
290	The commit and its PR remain the archive - the story of the incident, quoted exchanges and
291	session ids live there and in the capture, never in the rule and never in a canon's log. What
292	an entry takes from them is only the **reaffirmable core**: `Source` and `Reason`, the minimum
293	a future review needs to re-test the rule, and `Retire when`, the test it is reaffirmed
294	against. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument - a cost
295	the reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.
296	======
297	# research-project — running an algorithm against ground truth
298	
299	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
300	
301	For every substantive algorithmic change, in this order:
302	
303	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
304	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
305	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
306	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
307	   it** — do not guess.
308	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
309	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
310	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
311	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
312	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
313	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
314	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
315	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
316	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
317	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
318	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
319	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
320	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
321	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
322	
323	### Show, don't just tell
324	
325	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
326	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
327	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
328	
329	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
330	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
331	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
332	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
333	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
334	
335	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
336	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
337	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
338	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
339	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
340	
341	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
342	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
343	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
344	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
345	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
346	
347	- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
348	  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
349	  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
350	  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
351	  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
352	  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
353	  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
354	  trustworthy.
355	
356	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
357	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
358	
359	### Interaction cadence
360	
361	- **Keep the owner in the loop with pictures**, proactively, and ask a question only when a
362	  decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — never to confirm work you can
363	  verify yourself.
364	
365	- **Finishing a unit of work** — leave it committed and pushed, so it can be reviewed or
366	  resumed from a fresh session.
367	
368	---
369	
370	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
371	
372	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
373	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer — and never
374	  against the pipeline's own prior output, which validates nothing.
375	
376	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
377	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
378	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
379	
380	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
381	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
382	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
383	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
384	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
385	
386	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
387	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
388	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
389	  loudly.
390	
391	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
392	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
393	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
394	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
395	  are requirements, not incidental.
396	
397	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
398	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
399	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
400	  the review overlays.
401	
402	---
403	
404	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
405	
406	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
407	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
408	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
409	
410	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
411	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
412	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
413	
414	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
415	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
416	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
417	  in scope.
418	
419	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
420	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
421	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
422	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
423	
424	- **Choosing test images for a new detection/invariance harness** - default to real images
425	  already at hand (the uploaded corpus, literature figures) over a synthetic field; synthesize
426	  only once real options are exhausted. A synthetic image is built from the same assumptions the
427	  algorithm makes, so it tends to confirm the algorithm rather than test it.
428	
429	---
430	
431	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
432	
433	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
434	if it improves a metric.
435	
436	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
437	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
438	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
439	
440	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
441	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
442	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
443	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
444	
445	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
446	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
447	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
448	
449	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
450	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
451	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
452	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
453	
454	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
455	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
456	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
457	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
458	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
459	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
460	
461	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
462	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
463	
464	---
465	
466	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
467	
468	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
469	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
470	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
471	
472	An iteration note captures:
473	
474	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
475	  showed it).
476	
477	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
478	  possible).
479	
480	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
481	
482	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
483	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
484	
485	### A metric's definition is part of its identity
486	
487	Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
488	one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
489	silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
490	under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
491	definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
492	the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
493	the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
494	the failure this rule exists to prevent.
495	
496	### A raw measurement is comparable only inside one calibration
497	
498	When each input carries its own scale (a per-image conversion factor, a per-run
499	sampling rate, a per-source unit), a raw absolute quantity means something
500	different in every input. **Aggregate and compare only normalized quantities** —
501	a density, a ratio, a per-unit rate — never the raw number, and never a mean
502	spanning two sources that differ in more than scale (a different instrument,
503	subject or protocol changes *what* is measured, not just how much of it fits in
504	frame). Group the rollup by source and say what the grouping is for.
505	
506	The conversion factor is a **measurement of that input**, not a constant: read it
507	off the input itself, never infer it from a stated setting or borrow it from a
508	neighbour. It lives in exactly one place in the code — a second copy is a second
509	calibration, and whichever copy a given script happens to read wins silently. An
510	input offering nothing to measure the factor from is **not** quietly dropped:
511	mark it uncalibrated *with the reason*, report only its scale-free quantities,
512	and leave it visible as a known gap.
513	
514	### Definition of done for an accepted change
515	
516	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
517	
518	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
519	
520	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
521	
522	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
523	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
524	
525	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
526	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
527	  changed**.
528	
529	---
530	
531	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
532	
533	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
534	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
535	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
536	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
537	
538	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
539	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
540	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
541	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
542	
543	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
544	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
545	
546	---
547	
548	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
549	
550	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
551	
552	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
553	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
554	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
555	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
556	
557	- **Capture the method that exists only inside a figure.** Part of a source's
558	  actual procedure is often drawn rather than written — a panel's inset, an
559	  annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
560	  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
561	  until someone re-opens the source.
562	
563	- **Write down what the source *fails* to say**, as an explicit gap list — the
564	  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
565	  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
566	  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
567	  a stated gap is part of that.
568	
569	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
570	
571	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
572	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
573	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
574	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
575	
576	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
577	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
578	
579	---
580	
581	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
582	
583	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
584	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
585	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
586	
587	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
588	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
589	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
590	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
591	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
592	
593	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
594	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
595	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
596	
597	---
598	
599	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
600	
601	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
602	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
603	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
604	
605	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
606	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
607	
608	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
609	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
610	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
611	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
612	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
613	    nothing finer.
614	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
615	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
616	  mask-free validation path for those sets.
617	
618	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
619	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
620	  covered.
621	
622	---
623	
624	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
625	
626	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
627	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
628	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
629	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
630	
631	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
632	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
633	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
634	  exhausted first.
635	
636	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
637	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
638	  warm-up doc.
639	
640	---
641	
642	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
643	
644	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
645	first-class experiments:
646	
647	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
648	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
649	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
650	  couldn't.
651	
652	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
653	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
654	
655	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
656	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
657	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
658	  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
659	  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
660	  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
661	  the very structure you are measuring.
662	
663	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
664	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
665	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
666	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
667	
668	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
669	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
670	
671	---
672	
673	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
674	
675	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
676	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
677	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
678	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
679	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
680	substantially change a sub-step.
681	
682	---
683	
684	## 13. Continuity across sessions
685	
686	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
687	**resumable** state.
688	
689	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
690	  clean checkout.
691	
692	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
693	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
694	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
695	  codebase.
696	
697	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
698	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
699	  metrics current in it.
700	
701	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
702	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
703	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
704	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
705	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
706	  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
707	  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
708	  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
709	  isn't captured yet.
710	
711	- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
712	  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.
713	
714	---
715	
716	## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)
717	
718	Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
719	Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
720	such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
721	revived session:
722	
723	> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
724	> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
725	> the research task itself.**
726	> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
727	> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
728	> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
729	> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted
730	> on; how they want articles summarized, images extracted, and external data
731	> fetched; environment constraints they flagged; and how they hand off algorithm
732	> ideas. For each item, strip out anything specific to this project's subject
733	> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over
734	> similarly-formatted inputs, scored against user ground truth, improved in
735	> reviewable iterations." Then propose additions/edits to the relevant numbered
736	> section above (merge, don't duplicate; keep the principle-first phrasing). Show
737	> the owner a diff of what you'd add and confirm the wording before committing.
738	> **Do not run or modify the research pipeline.** If a preference contradicts what
739	> is already written here, surface the conflict for the owner rather than silently
740	> overwriting.
741	
742	To make revival productive, when the owner asks for it they should say **which
743	session(s)** to revive (a link or a description) and, if possible, what topic the
744	process discussion centred on — so the revived session knows where in the
745	transcript to look.
746	research-project:
747	README.md
748	RULES.md
749	badge.svg
750	pack.mjs
751	// no-rfinder — this repo's own pack: everything local, and portable nowhere. Its rules,
752	// and the checks, skills and tasks that carry them, all live here.
753	// A lesson that would hold in another repo belongs in a canon pack instead — propose it
754	// upstream.
755	//
756	// The id is this directory's name and the prose is the RULES.md beside this file —
757	// both by convention (engine/pack_loader/pack-conventions.mjs), so neither is
758	// declared here.
759	export default {
760	  version: 1,
761	  ruleRoutingGuidance: {
762	    belongs: 'everything specific to this repository and portable nowhere else: its working rules, and the checks, skills and tasks carrying them',
763	    excludes: 'anything true beyond this repo — that belongs in a canon pack, proposed upstream',
764	  },
765	  detect: null,
766	  marker: null,
767	  worldRules: [],
768	  // The image ships no scientific Python, so every session otherwise re-installs it before it
769	  // can run the detector or its invariance test. Declared here rather than in the web pack's
770	  // setup body, which is generic for every project.
771	  //
772	  // requirements.txt is the single place the dependency set is named -- listing the packages
773	  // again here would be a second copy to drift.
774	  env: {
775	    label: 'Python imaging stack (numpy, scipy, pillow, matplotlib)',
776	    setup: 'python3 -m pip install --quiet --root-user-action=ignore -r requirements.txt',
777	    probe: 'python3 -c "import numpy, scipy, PIL, matplotlib" >/dev/null 2>&1',
778	  },
779	};
